new_statements.quote: 5. Während der Vokalismus beider Mundarten keine nennenswerten Verschiedenheiten aufweist, liegt in der von Maṅga der Ton gern dem Ende des Wortes näher als in der von Gāzir. So budú Gras = K. búdu, žení kleine Kalabasse = K. tšéni, gaṅgáma Trommler = K. gáṅgāma, gāfẹlí Hirse = K. ṅgáfẹli, kašágar Schwert = K. kásagar (B. kasákkar). Die Hauptbelege liefert die Formenlehre. Indessen ist zu bemerken, daß der dynamische Akzent, auch wo er sich mit dem musikalischen vereint, im Bornu wie im Haussa nicht derart hervortritt wie in den europäischen und semitischen Sprachen. Oft liegen die Silben eines Wortes anscheinend im Gleichgewicht oder es ist der Satz- bzw. Versrhythmus, der sie gliedert.
new_statements.translation: 5. While the vowel systems of the two dialects show no differences worth mentioning, in the Manga dialect the accent tends to lie nearer the end of the word than in the Gazir dialect [Koelle 1854]. Thus budú 'grass' = K. búdu, žení 'small calabash' = K. tšéni, gaṅgáma 'drummer' = K. gáṅgāma, gāfẹlí 'millet' = K. ṅgáfẹli, kašágar 'sword' = K. kásagar (B. kasákkar). The main evidence comes from the morphology. It should be noted, however, that the dynamic (stress) accent, even where it combines with the musical (pitch) accent, does not stand out in Bornu [Kanuri], as in Hausa, the way it does in the European and Semitic languages. Often the syllables of a word are apparently in equilibrium, or it is the sentence or verse rhythm that organizes them.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Prietze (impressionistic, 1914, one Manga speaker from Bursari): word prominence in Manga Kanuri tends toward the end of the word (often the final syllable) where Koelle's Gazir Kanuri has it earlier; but stress as such is weak — syllables of a word often sound evenly weighted and grouping is by sentence/verse rhythm, so he declined to mark accent on every word. Modern Manga lexicography (Jarrett 2007) marks lexical tone on every syllable, i.e. the variety is tonal like other Kanuri; no modern source accessible states a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 137: Manga tends to stress the verbal endings ži/či (perfect sg.), žina/čina, žana/čana (participial), žia/čia (conjunctional), where in Koelle's and Barth's Kanuri the accent precedes the ending; 2sg imperative -e usually accented in Manga (never in Koelle's conj. I); 2pl imperative -ogo/-ago etc. 'bei schwebender Betonung' (level/hovering stress); p. 138 plural suffix -wa 'im M. meist betont'. Prietze also notes (p. 136) that his accent marks waver between word accent and verse accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Observations drawn from dictated song texts and speech of a single informant (al-Hajj Musa ibn Hissein, b. Bursari, Manga district; Awagana & Lefebvre 2025: 18-19 note his Kanuri mixes Manga and some Yerwa traits). Prietze explicitly says word-level accent is often overridden by sentence/verse rhythm; 'Ton'/'Akzent' are used pre-tonologically (1914), not as a tone analysis. A French translation of the same passage is in Awagana & Lefebvre 2025: 93, 95 (saved), which mistranslates the 'nearer the word end' clause.
new_statements.identity_note: Prietze 1914 describes the 'Mangadialekt' as spoken by one informant, al-Hajj Musa ibn Hissein, born in Bursari (Manga district of Borno, today Yobe State, Nigeria), contrasted throughout with Koelle's 1854 Gazir Kanuri; Awagana & Lefebvre 2025: 18-19 note his speech is basically Manga (western Kanuri, mang1399) with some Yerwa (cent2050) traits. Jarrett 2007 and the Peace Corps 1993 manual represent Niger Manga (Mainé-Soroa/Diffa region), same glottocode mang1399. Awobuluyi 1969 is Yerwa (Central Kanuri, cent2050) and is cited only as context.

sources.note: Einleitung A ('Die lautlichen Besonderheiten des Mangadialekts'), point 5, pp. 135-136: in Manga the accent ('der Ton') tends to lie nearer the end of the word than in Koelle's Gazir dialect (budú = K. búdu, zení = K. tšéni, gangáma = K. gángāma, gafəlí = K. ngáfeli, kaságar = K. kásagar); but the dynamic accent, even where it combines with the musical one, does not stand out in Kanuri (or Hausa) as in European/Semitic languages; often the syllables of a word seem to be in equilibrium, or it is sentence/verse rhythm that organizes them; hence his reluctance to mark accent on every word. p. 13…

sources.citation: Peace Corps Niger. 1993. Manuel de Kanuri. Niamey: Peace Corps. 89 pp. (ERIC ED401747).
sources.note: Image-only scan, now fully scanned (tesseract). Manga-type vocabulary; no pronunciation, tone or stress section anywhere; only p. 11 'Questions are made by adding wa to the final word or merely raising the tone'.

sources.citation: Awagana, Ari & Camille Lefebvre. 2025. L'œuvre en kanouri d'al-Hajj Musa ibn Hissein, un savant du Borno (Niger-Nigéria). Leiden: Brill (open access), 525 pp.
sources.note: Contains a French translation of Prietze's 1914 Einleitung: the accent passage is on p. 93 (pdf p. 114) and the accented-endings remark on p. 95 (pdf p. 116); the translation garbles the 'nearer the word end' clause. Editors' own text: pp. 18-19 Manga (with Dagara) = western branch of Kanuri, al-Hajj Musa (b. Bursari, Manga district) speaks Manga with some Yerwa traits; p. 64 Prietze's tone marking is inconsistent, partly tonal partly intonational; fn. 290 (p. 66) 'La métrique et la prosodie kanouri sont très mal connues'. No stress rule of their own.

sources.citation: Jarrett, Kevin. 2007. A dictionary of Manga, a Kanuri language of Eastern Niger and NE Nigeria. Ed. Roger Blench. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 162 pp.
sources.note: Every headword carries tone marks (acute, grave, circumflex, hacek) i.e. lexical tone on each syllable; front matter is Blench's one-page introduction only ('Tone-marks sometimes omitted'); no statement on stress or accent.

sources.note: Mainé-Soroa (Manga) is one of the test dialects; only a general remark that tone is not written in the orthography; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Awobuluyi, A. Oladele et al. 1969. Introductory Kanuri / Introduction au kanouri. Washington DC: Center for Applied Linguistics / Peace Corps. 606 pp. (ERIC ED051717).
sources.note: NOT Manga (Yerwa/Maiduguri dialect). Pronunciation drills (pdf p. ~54): acute = high tone, grave = low tone; 'Syllables with the high tone in Kanuri are not the same as accented syllables in English. It is therefore necessary to remember not to pronounce such Kanuri syllable with extra force'. No word-stress rule.
